subtitle: Distinguish Sudanese and South Sudanese Minnesotans, describe their many peoples, languages and faiths, and plan DHS service that meets current needs without asking people to recount conflict.
audience: For all DHS and DSD employees, including case managers, eligibility, data, policy and communications staff, who serve Sudanese or South Sudanese individuals and families or partner with their community and faith organizations.

lessons.title: Two countries, a shared and difficult history
objectives: Summarize the main conflicts that led to displacement from Sudan and South Sudan.
Distinguish Sudan and South Sudan as separate countries since South Sudan's independence.
Describe how Sudanese and South Sudanese communities formed in Minnesota.
Explain why arrival data list most early arrivals under Sudan.
lessons.teaching:
Sudan became independent in the mid-nineteen-fifties, and for most of the decades that followed, the country was at war with itself. Southern Sudanese, many of them Christian or following traditional beliefs, fought the Arab-led, mostly Muslim government in the north over political power, religion, land and later oil. The second civil war, which began in the early nineteen-eighties, killed an estimated two million people and displaced about four million. By the early nineteen-nineties, around half a million Sudanese refugees were living in camps in Ethiopia and Kenya. A peace agreement in the mid-two-thousands ended the north-south war, and in the early twenty-tens South Sudan voted overwhelmingly for independence and became a new country.

Conflict did not end. Within about two years of independence, fighting broke out in South Sudan between Dinka and Nuer members of the presidential guard and spread into a civil war that displaced millions. In Sudan, the Darfur region endured years of violence against Fur, Masalit, Zaghawa and other communities. More recently, war between the Sudanese Armed Forces and the Rapid Support Forces has driven what Minority Rights Group describes as roughly twelve million people from their homes, including more than four million who fled to neighboring countries.

Minnesota's communities formed in waves. The Department of Health's cumulative table counts more than 1,100 primary refugee arrivals from Sudan, with the largest numbers in the mid-to-late nineteen-nineties and early two-thousands. Carleton College's Religions in Minnesota project describes about four hundred Nuer settling in the Twin Cities during the nineteen-nineties, some resettled directly and others moving here from other states to join community. Dinka families built a congregation in Rochester. Because South Sudan did not exist as a country until recently, earlier South Sudanese arrivals appear in the data under Sudan. The table lists only about one hundred arrivals under South Sudan, most in the last two years. In the most recent state report, there were 59 new arrivals from Sudan and 43 from South Sudan.

The lesson for staff is to ask, not assume. A person born in what is now South Sudan may have documents that say Sudan. A person from Sudan may be from Khartoum, Darfur or the Nuba Mountains, with very different histories. Let people tell you which country and community they identify with.
lessons.keyPoint: Sudan and South Sudan are separate countries with a shared history of long wars. Many South Sudanese Minnesotans arrived when their homeland was still part of Sudan, so documents and data may not match how they identify.
lessons.example: Fictional case: Akol, a man in his forties who came to Minnesota as a young refugee, calls a DHS unit to update his information. The worker, Jenna, sees that his record lists country of birth as Sudan and says, so you are Sudanese. Akol pauses and says he is South Sudanese, from a Dinka family, and that his papers were issued before independence. Jenna's screen only offers the country names in a list.
lessons.question: What should Jenna do?
choices: Explain that his document says Sudan, so that is what he is.
Change his country of birth to South Sudan without checking the program's rules.
Apologize for the assumption, explain what the field records, follow program guidance on whether and how it can be updated, and use any available self-identification field.
feedback: Telling Akol what his identity is based on an old document dismisses him and repeats a painful history. Country of birth on a document and identity are different things.
Changing an official data field without following the program's rules could create a mismatch with his documents. The right process matters, even when the intent is good.
This is the strongest choice. It repairs the moment, is honest about what the field means, follows the rules, and makes room for how Akol identifies.
lessons.reflection: When a person's identity does not match the categories your system offers, how do you usually respond? What would you like to say next time?
lessons.action: Check whether the forms and systems you use list Sudan and South Sudan separately and include any self-identification field. Note any gap and send it to the form or system owner.

check.question: Why are many South Sudanese Minnesotans counted under Sudan in older refugee arrival data?
check.correct: They arrived before South Sudan became an independent country, when their homeland was part of Sudan.
wrong: Because South Sudanese and Sudanese are the same community.
Because the state does not collect country of origin for refugees.
check.feedback: South Sudan became independent only in the early twenty-tens. People who fled the southern region earlier were recorded as from Sudan. Data categories often lag behind history, so let people identify themselves.

lessons.title: Many peoples, many languages
objectives: Describe the ethnic and linguistic diversity of Sudan and South Sudan.
Identify languages that Sudanese and South Sudanese Minnesotans may prefer, including Arabic, Dinka and Nuer.
Explain why an Arabic interpreter is not automatically right for a person from either country.
Plan an interpreter request that accounts for language and conflict history.
lessons.teaching:
Both countries are among the most diverse in Africa. Minority Rights Group describes Sudan as home to more than five hundred ethnic groups speaking over four hundred languages. Arabic is the official language and widely spoken, and many Sudanese identify as Arab. Others belong to groups such as the Nubians in the north, the Beja in the east, the Fur, Masalit and Zaghawa of Darfur, and the many peoples of the Nuba Mountains, each with their own languages. Most Sudanese are Muslim, and there are Christian communities as well.

South Sudan has more than seventy languages. The Dinka are the largest group, followed by the Nuer, with many others including the Shilluk, Murle, Azande and Bari. Christianity and traditional beliefs are the most common faiths, and some South Sudanese are Muslim. Many South Sudanese also speak Arabic, often a local form of it, as well as English, which became an official language after independence. People who grew up in refugee camps in Kenya or Ethiopia may speak Swahili or Amharic too.

For language access, the name of the country tells you very little. A Sudanese person from Darfur may prefer Arabic for official business but speak Fur or Masalit at home. A South Sudanese elder may be most comfortable in Dinka or Nuer. Dinka and Nuer are distinct languages, and each has several dialects. Assigning an Arabic interpreter to someone because they are from Sudan or South Sudan can leave them struggling to follow, especially on complex topics like health care, disability services or appeals.

Conflict history can also matter. Some fighting in South Sudan has followed Dinka and Nuer lines, and violence in Darfur targeted specific groups. Most people will work fine with any qualified interpreter, and most interpreters are neutral professionals. Still, some may be uneasy about an interpreter from a group associated with the violence they fled, or about confidentiality in a close community. Ask every person the same neutral questions: What language would you like to use? Is this interpreter a good fit for you? Honor requests for a different interpreter without asking for a reason.
lessons.keyPoint: Country names do not tell you a person's language. Ask about preferred language, which may be Arabic, Dinka, Nuer or one of many others, and whether the interpreter is a good fit.
lessons.example: Fictional case: Nyakuoth, a South Sudanese grandmother raising her grandchildren, attends a meeting about a child's disability services. The county booked an Arabic interpreter because the referral listed South Sudan. Nyakuoth answers in a mix of Nuer and a few Arabic words, and her adult nephew begins translating from Nuer to English on the side. The worker, Pat, is not sure who to listen to.
lessons.question: What should Pat do?
choices: Pause, confirm Nyakuoth's preferred language, and reschedule or switch to a qualified Nuer interpreter, by phone or video if needed.
Continue with the Arabic interpreter, since Nyakuoth understands some Arabic.
Let the nephew take over interpreting, since he speaks both Nuer and English.
feedback: This is the strongest choice. It fixes the mismatch at its source and gives Nyakuoth qualified interpretation in her language for important decisions about a child.
Understanding some Arabic is not the same as understanding complex service information. Continuing risks decisions she has not fully understood.
The nephew may be helpful, but relying on a relative can affect accuracy and privacy, and it is not a substitute for a qualified interpreter in a formal meeting.
lessons.reflection: What information do you usually have about a person's language before a first meeting? How could you learn more before the meeting instead of during it?
lessons.action: Look up how your unit requests Dinka and Nuer interpreters, including phone and video options, and how much notice is needed. Save the details where your team can find them.

check.question: A referral says a family is from South Sudan. What is the best way to choose an interpreter?
check.correct: Ask the family which language they prefer, since it may be Dinka, Nuer, Arabic, English or another language.
wrong: Book an Arabic interpreter, since Arabic is spoken in both Sudan and South Sudan.
Book an English speaker, since English is an official language of South Sudan.
check.feedback: South Sudan has more than seventy languages, and official language status does not tell you what a person speaks best. Ask directly, and record the answer for future contacts.

lessons.title: Family, faith and community life
objectives: Describe how extended family and kinship can shape households and decisions.
Identify the role of faith communities as community hubs for many families.
Explain how naming and date-of-birth differences can appear in records.
Draft neutral questions about who is part of a household and who should be involved.
lessons.teaching:
For many Sudanese and South Sudanese families, family means more than parents and children. Aunts, uncles, cousins and grandparents often carry responsibility for one another. War and displacement strengthened this. Children were often raised by relatives when parents were killed, separated or far away, and many young people grew up in camps with extended family or peers. Today, a household may include nieces, nephews or grandchildren, and caregiving arrangements may not match what paperwork shows. Elders are often respected as decision-makers, and families may want to consult relatives before agreeing to a plan. These are patterns shaped by many cultures and experiences, so ask each family about its own arrangements.

Faith communities are central for many families. Carleton College's Religions in Minnesota project describes Nuer Minnesotans founding Nile Our Savior Lutheran Church. In Rochester, a Dinka congregation has worshipped with Zumbro Lutheran Church since the mid-two-thousands, holding services in Dinka. Many South Sudanese are Christian and belong to a range of churches, including Lutheran congregations, while many Sudanese are Muslim and connect through mosques and Sudanese community associations. Churches and mosques are often where people share news, organize help and welcome newcomers, which makes them valuable partners for outreach. Not everyone is religious, and no one should be expected to receive services through a faith organization.

Records may raise questions. Names from Arabic, Dinka, Nuer and other languages can be spelled several ways in English. Name order on documents may reflect how an official recorded it rather than how the person uses it, and family members may have different last names. Many people who were displaced as children do not know their exact date of birth, so documents sometimes carry estimated dates, and January first is often recorded when the real date is unknown. These are not signs of error or fraud.

Ask simple questions. Who lives in your household? Who helps care for the children? Who would you like involved in this decision? How should your name be written? Then follow the program's rules for household composition, which rely on who lives and shares expenses together, not on shared surnames or standard family shapes.
lessons.keyPoint: Extended family and faith communities are central for many families. Households and records may not look the way forms expect, and that is not a problem with the family.
lessons.example: Fictional case: Grace, a DSD program specialist, is reviewing a support plan for Deng, a young man with a disability who lives with his uncle, aunt and several cousins. The plan lists the uncle as the main support person, but the original referral named Deng's mother, who lives in another state. A colleague suggests the plan is inconsistent and that Grace should require the mother's signature on all decisions. Deng is an adult.
lessons.question: What should Grace do?
choices: Require the mother's signature, since she is Deng's closest relative.
Talk with Deng about who he wants involved, confirm any legal decision-making arrangements through proper documentation, and update the plan to reflect his choices.
Remove the uncle from the plan until the family clarifies its structure.
feedback: Deng is an adult, and closeness in a family chart does not create decision-making authority. Requiring a signature he has not chosen could override his rights.
This is the strongest choice. It centers Deng's own choices, checks any formal authority through documentation rather than assumptions, and respects the family arrangement that actually supports him.
Removing the person who provides day-to-day support could harm Deng and misreads a common extended-family arrangement as confusion.
lessons.reflection: What picture of family do the forms and plans you use assume? Who might that picture leave out?
lessons.action: Review one plan or form template you use. Check whether it lets people name support people beyond parents and spouses. If not, suggest wording that lets a person list anyone they choose.

check.question: A refugee's documents show January first as their birthday, and a sibling's documents show the same date in a different year. What is the most likely explanation?
check.correct: Exact birth dates were unknown and estimated dates were recorded, a common practice for displaced people.
wrong: The siblings must be twins recorded incorrectly.
check.feedback: Many people displaced by war, especially as children, do not know their exact birth date. Estimated dates are common and not a sign of fraud. Follow the program's rules for identity verification.

lessons.title: Service barriers and respectful practice
objectives: Identify service barriers facing both long-settled and recently arrived Sudanese and South Sudanese Minnesotans.
Explain why staff should not ask people to recount conflict or displacement.
Distinguish required information from unnecessary questions about status or ethnicity.
Plan a referral list that includes legal, resettlement and community resources.
lessons.teaching:
Sudanese and South Sudanese Minnesotans include people who arrived as children decades ago and now raise families, run businesses and lead congregations here, as well as people who arrived in the past year or two. Barriers differ. Long-settled families may face language barriers among elders, caregiving for aging relatives, or disability and health needs linked to hard early lives. Recent arrivals may be navigating housing, work, schools and benefits for the first time, often after years in camps or cities in neighboring countries.

The current war in Sudan weighs heavily on many families, whatever their arrival date. A community organizer quoted in the Minnesota Spokesman-Recorder described the strain of surviving here while supporting relatives there, saying she did not know who she would send money to that month. People may be sending much of their income abroad, trying to locate relatives, or grieving losses. Continuing instability in South Sudan has similar effects. This stress can show up as missed appointments, financial hardship or exhaustion, and it deserves patience rather than judgment.

Many people lived through violence, flight and loss. Do not ask anyone to describe what happened to them, how they escaped, or what they saw, unless a specific authorized process requires it and trained staff are doing it. Do not ask about ethnicity to guess someone's side in a conflict. Do not make comments about who was responsible for violence. If someone chooses to share, listen, acknowledge it, and return to what they need now. Collect immigration status only when a program rule requires it. Sudanese and South Sudanese Minnesotans hold many different statuses, some of them temporary and subject to federal change, and status questions belong with immigration legal services.

Respectful practice rests on a few good questions and good referrals. What language would you like to use? Is this interpreter a good fit? Who would you like involved? What would help most right now? Refer to the DHS Resettlement Programs Office and its Refugee and Immigrant Helpline for resettlement services, to immigration legal providers for status questions, and to community and faith organizations when the person wants that connection.
lessons.keyPoint: Meet current needs with patience and clear referrals. War at home can shape daily life here, but people should never be asked to recount conflict or reveal status the service does not need.
lessons.example: Fictional case: Amani, a Sudanese woman who arrived about a year ago, has missed two appointments for her son's disability assessment. When Kyle, the case manager, reaches her by phone with an Arabic interpreter, she apologizes and says her family in Sudan has been displaced and she has been trying to reach them. Kyle's supervisor has asked him to document the reason for missed appointments. Kyle wants to be accurate and kind.
lessons.question: What should Kyle do?
choices: Ask Amani for details about what happened to her family so he can document the situation fully.
Tell Amani that repeated missed appointments may close the case, so she needs to prioritize it.
Acknowledge her situation briefly, record a short neutral note such as family emergency, offer flexible scheduling or a phone option, and mention support resources if she wants them.
feedback: Detailed questions about her family's displacement are not needed for the record and could cause distress. A short neutral note meets the documentation need.
Program rules about missed appointments matter, but leading with a warning ignores what she just shared and may push her away from services her son needs.
This is the strongest choice. It documents what is needed without intrusive detail, adjusts the process to her circumstances, and leaves the choice about further support with her.
lessons.reflection: How do you document sensitive reasons for missed appointments or delays? What is the least detail that still meets the need?
lessons.action: Write two or three neutral phrases you could use in case notes to record a family emergency or hardship without recording traumatic details. Check them against your program's documentation guidance.

check.question: A person from South Sudan mentions they are Nuer. What is the most respectful response from a DHS worker?
check.correct: Note it if the person wants it recorded and relevant, such as for language, and do not ask about their experience of the conflict.
wrong: Ask how the conflict between Dinka and Nuer affected their family.
Assign an interpreter from a different ethnic group to stay neutral.
check.feedback: Ethnic identity can matter for language and community connections, but it is not an invitation to discuss the conflict. Ask about language and interpreter comfort neutrally, and let the person lead.

cards.back: Two separate countries since South Sudan's independence in the early twenty-tens. Earlier South Sudanese arrivals are often recorded as from Sudan.
The two largest peoples of South Sudan, each with its own language and dialects. Many Dinka and Nuer families live in Minnesota.
A region of western Sudan whose Fur, Masalit, Zaghawa and other communities have endured years of violence. People from Darfur may speak Arabic and their own languages.
Dates recorded when a person's exact birth date is unknown, often January first. A common result of displacement, not a sign of error or fraud.
Moving to Minnesota after first resettling in another state. Many Sudanese and South Sudanese families came this way, so arrival data undercount them.

aid.heading: Language and interpreters
items: Ask preferred language; do not assume Arabic from the country name.
Know how to request Dinka, Nuer and other language interpreters by phone or video.
Ask whether the interpreter is a good fit and honor requests for a change.
Do not rely on relatives or children to interpret in formal meetings.

aid.heading: Identity, family and records
items: Let people identify as Sudanese or South Sudanese, regardless of old documents.
Ask who lives in the household and who the person wants involved.
Treat estimated birth dates and name variations as normal.
Follow program rules for household composition, not assumptions about family shape.

aid.heading: Respect and referral
items: Do not ask people to recount conflict, flight or losses.
Do not ask about ethnicity to guess someone's side in a conflict.
Collect immigration status only when a program rule requires it.
Refer to the Refugee and Immigrant Helpline, immigration legal services, and community or faith organizations when the person wants that.
